utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic, representing the Defence for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague, Mr. Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey and, along with my esteemed colleague, Ms. Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. SENAD BEGTASOVIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Let me solve a small technical problem here. Thank you, everything is fine now. Good morning, Mr. Begtasovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you manage to rest a little bit over the weekend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, I would like to continue where we left off on Friday. You will recall that, before this Trial Chamber, on Friday you identified a number of statements which you took from individuals who were in Celebici and who were later transferred to Musala; do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated before the Trial Chamber that you reviewed files of other individuals who had been detained in Celebici and relating to this issue, Mr. Begtasovic, could you tell the Trial Chamber what was in the files which you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that I did not review these files very carefully. That is the files that I had access to. I recall that these were statements for the most part of the same suspects whom I had interviewed and this was part of a proceeding that was -- which took place prior to the proceedings in which I was involved, and as I recall, these persons had been interviewed in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Beside the statements which you glanced at, if not thoroughly reviewed, were there any other documents there that you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that there were decisions on release from detention of some of these individuals, that is, the measures of detentions were abolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you recall from what period such decisions were dated, given that you interviewed the suspects in January 1993, so from which period were the decisions that you reviewed -- what period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only recall that they were from the summer of 1992. I could not give you a more precise time frame.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, can you tell us whether, by reviewing these documents, you were able to determine how many individuals were released, taking into account that you pointed out that you did not review them very carefully or very thoroughly, but can you tell us was it a small number, was it a larger number of individuals who were released at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At any rate, it was a larger number of people and, when I say a larger number, then as a parameter I can take a number of persons whom I subsequently interviewed, so that means that there would be several dozen individuals. How many exactly, I could not tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, can you remember individuals who signed these documents on release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that I mentioned that before, that is, last time I testified. As I recall, those decisions were signed by Mr. Lokas, Mr. Zovko, and I cannot recall who else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Begtasovic. As a member of the commission, you interviewed these individuals and you gave us a fairly accurate number of 105. Can you please tell this Trial Chamber whether, in questioning these individuals, you were able to determine whether these persons possessed arms or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost all interviewed persons did have weapons -- at least, that is what they stated to me. It is possible that, out of 105 individuals who were questioned -- and this is the number that I recall -- there were maybe two or three individuals who did not possess weapons -- at least that is what they stated to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I please ask the usher's assistance to show the witness the document on the appointment of the commission -- it is D7/1 and I again apologise to the court for not having had enough copies on Friday for their Honours and for the witness, so now we have a sufficient number of copies, so can the copies please be handed out to everyone. (Handed) Mr. Begtasovic, have you reviewed this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the order whereby your commission was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And (1) are all the members named, including yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, since the witness recognises the document order by which he was appointed a member of the commission, I move to admit it into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any objection? I am not sure that this has not been tendered before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document was marked for identification through one of the Prosecution witnesses, but I was informed by the Registry that it had not been admitted into evidence, so now I would like to move to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Begtasovic, given the fact that, as a member of the commission, you questioned the mentioned individuals, as a judge were you able to determine at that time, and taking into account all the facts that they conveyed to you, did you come to a determination whether criminal proceedings should be instigated against these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What criminal charges would be appropriate based on the facts that you determined by questioning these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basic criminal act which was -- for which there was suspicion based on the facts that I determined was armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, as a very experienced criminal judge, can you tell this Trial Chamber what punishment was foreseen for crime of this kind during the wartime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For such a crime which was committed either in wartime or in a situation of the threat of armed conflict, the punishment was the most severe punishment, which was set out by the SFRY law, which had been adopted by the Bosnian authorities for these crimes which was the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, for crimes for which the death penalty is the highest available sentence, is detention an obligatory measure for persons who were charged with such a crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pursuant to the law, detention is obligatory -- it is mandatory. There is no possibility of not having a detention in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, can you tell us how long may a suspect be detained legally during the investigation process before the indictment is issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The investigating judge can order a 30-day detention and, from there on, until the investigation is completed, the trial chamber can order detention for up to six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, what happens after the indictment has been issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The trial chamber, that is not the pre-trial judge, can determine to order to continue with the detention and it reviews it every two months. After the trial, after the sentencing, if the sentence is more than five years, then the case can be reviewed again and then we start from zero.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, given your investigation, in your opinion, as a person who is both an experienced criminal judge and a person who was investigating these persons, was detention of persons who were charged with crimes which you just mentioned justified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given the fact that these individuals possessed weapons illegally, that they engaged in acts which were directed against the system, given the fact that there was enough grounds, that there was suspicion that they engaged in these acts, that all means that there were grounds for their detention.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even though you mentioned this on Friday, let me ask you again, Mr. Begtasovic: do you know how the proceedings against these individuals whom you questioned were completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that certain persons were later prosecuted and I also do not know how many such proceedings took place, but I know that all proceedings were later abolished through a decision adopted by the court based on the law of amnesty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, by dropping charges pursuant to the law of amnesty, does this mean that these people were pardoned or does this mean something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the court does not take a decision on whether these individuals did commit such acts or not. The court only acknowledges that they have fulfilled conditions that meet the law of amnesty. It would be the same as when an application is made for a pardon -- it is an act of mercy on the part of the authorities to pardon a convicted person, or a person who is being prosecuted regardless of the fact whether this person actually did commit such a crime or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, on Friday you said that the court which was able to prosecute for a more serious crime, that it was established only during 1993. Can you tell me whether, at that time, criminal charges were filed against some other individuals who may have committed some other different crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A large number of indictments were issued against a variety of individuals in the military court in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, do you know whether, at that time, indictments were issued against individuals who committed crimes, the victims of whom were also certain persons of Serbian ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a number of such criminal cases that were processed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Begtasovic, when you questioned these individuals, can you tell us where did these people reside before the war, that is, before the hostilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority lived in the territory of the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your questioning of these individuals, Mr. Begtasovic, were you able to determine what citizenship these individuals held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, how do you legally determine the citizenship of an individual in Bosnia-Herzegovina; in other words, what was the underlying legal act for determining citizenship of anyone in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be by birth certificate and there was an office in the municipality in Konjic which had a register of citizens and I believe that this was so since 1979. Before that, the procedure was a bit different, so there was no separate list of citizens until then and then, after that, it was part of the Registry of births and deaths.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, did the legal system in Bosnia-Herzegovina provide for the citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was set out in the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, who can be issued with a birth certificate, that is a citizenship certificate which, as you said, are all being registered in the place of residence of individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whoever has a legal interest to be issued such a document and who can provide the authorities with good reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I have the usher's assistance to help me show the witness a document which was produced by Professor Hadzibegovic, and I am not asking for this witness to confirm the truthfulness of this document, but, rather, just to be able to answer several questions that I have to pose. I have a copy -- an original for Mr. Begtasovic, if you would please hand it to him. (Handed)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document D160/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, did you look at the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document represents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a certificate of citizenship issued by the registry in Konjic -- the municipal registry. Today, this is not a valid certificate, because there is an old coat of arms with lilies, which is no longer in use. Also, the name of the State is Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Today, it is only Bosnia-Herzegovina, so with the exception of these two details, everything else is the same today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, can you tell me whether such certificates were being issued up until the end of last year, that is, with that name and that coat of arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, such certificates were being issued until the end of last year and they were valid for legal purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether an attorney for a certain person who has an interest in such matters needs to ask proper authorities for issuance of such a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, an attorney who has the right legal interest can be issued such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I move to admit this into evidence -- not on whether this is Milan Kuljanin's citizenship certificate, but in terms of the truthfulness of what the judge has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think you can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, in that case this exhibit has been admitted and we will try to determine its truthfulness through other witnesses. Mr. Begtasovic, on Friday you told us about your court, which did not function throughout the whole of 1992, and the reasons for this. Tell us, please, apart from the courts like your own and the higher court, are there any other administrative courts in the municipality, or in the municipalities in keeping with our regulations -- do any other courts exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You have municipal courts for misdemeanours, for smaller crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is the difference between that type of court and the courts in the jurisdiction system of the republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the difference is in their competencies and authorities. This type of court deals with decision-making on smaller crimes if a misdemeanour has been committed and punishments and penalties for those types of crime. The difference is also in the selection of the judges. The judges of the municipal courts are elected by the municipal assemblies -- at least what were the municipal assemblies in the former system of the time -- and those are administrative courts, so to speak, which are linked up with the municipal organs of management, or with the municipal powers that be. As opposed to this type of court, we have the basic courts in the municipalities, which are hierarchically linked to the higher court and the supreme court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The competency and authority over the regularity of these regular courts is done by the Ministry of Justice and jurisprudence and authority over the municipal courts for the misdemeanours and petty crimes is done by the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, before the war, tell me, please, which were the organs of the municipal assembly over which it had superiority -- superior authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, the executive board, as the executive organ of power and authority of the municipal assembly, and the organs of management. There were a certain number of secretariats -- I forget their exact number, four or five I believe -- and the municipal court for misdemeanours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me to whom the Serb station of public security was subordinate before the war and during the war as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both before the war and in the course of the war, it was subject to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the republican Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, do you have personal knowledge from your practice to whom were subordinated the departments for national defence which were formerly known as the secretariats for national Defence, who were they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the republican Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that Dr. Iljas Hadzibegovic made up a chart of pre-war organisation of power and authority in the municipality, which is to be found in our dossiers on page 290 and 291 -- that is, the Bosnian text and translation -- I would like to show the witness this chart, this diagram. (Handed) Without looking this document up in our volume, in our big volume, I have a copy for the court.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is D161/1, Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, on the basis of your personal knowledge and experience, can you tell us whether this diagram represents the organisation of the organs and their subordinate organs within the municipality of Konjic before the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this diagram is, for the most part, correct, I would say. I should just like to mention that, as far as the communication between the basic courts is concerned -- and I said that a moment ago -- with the higher courts and the supreme court, there is another parallel link between the basic court and the ministry of jurisprudence, of justice, of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the organisational sense, but this is the pre-war organisation in the municipality as it stood and it is a correct diagram.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that, based on his personal experience, the witness is well acquainted with the makeup of the organisation of power and authority in the municipality, I move that this diagram be accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why? He did not produce this. It is not his own efforts, and he is making only a claim that he knows that such a thing exists. It is not him who produced it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, listening to Professor Hadzibegovic, who made up this diagram and identified it, we have just the verisimilitude of the diagram. The witness has identified Professor Hadzibegovic -- he did not have any personal knowledge of the functions of this kind of work in Konjic, but, as we now have the fact that somebody has identified the diagram and has somebody else who is well acquainted with the organisation of power and authority, in view of the relevance of this document, I submit that it be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you not think you are misunderstanding the situation? If you are introducing a matter as an exhibit produced by you, obviously there would be no problem tendering it as produced by you. If he is giving evidence because he knows about the system in which he works, go ahead and ask him whatever questions you want -- I do not think anybody bothers about that. If he said things which shows he knows about the system, it is sufficient, not because he is now adopting this diagram as his own -- this is what tendering it will mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is merely verifying its correctness -- nothing more than that. The document will have to be exhibited from Dr Iljas Hadzibegovic. He is merely confirming that it is a true representation -- that is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You seem to misunderstand how it works. All we are saying here is that the professor has tendered it as a document produced by him. Your witness is now saying this document represents accurately what he knows this system to be. This is all he can do, and no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. I have understood your Honours' warning. The witness has testified to its correctness -- verified its correctness and that it is a true representation and that is contained in the transcript of this court. Mr. Begtasovic, I should now like to ask you to tell me what happens with the municipal assembly as an organ of power and authority in a situation of war and the direct threat and danger of war? Does this organ experience any changes and who performs the function of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of an objective impossibility of convening an assembly at this particular time, and due to the war circumstances prevailing, the function of the municipal assembly was taken over, as far as I recall, in April 1992 by the war presidency of the municipality of Konjic. Everything that the municipal assembly dealt with, all the matters that it dealt with before the war, were now dealt with by the war-time presidency of the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, tell us, please, whether, after the proclamation of the immediate dangers of war, during the war in Konjic, whether there was a Territorial Defence headquarters, which later became the headquarters of the armed forces and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, from your personal experience as somebody who lived and worked in Konjic in 1992, to whom the headquarters of Territorial Defence of Konjic was subordinate -- who was the superior authority to the headquarters of Konjic's Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The republican headquarters of Territorial Defence were the superior authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We already had that from a number of witnesses, including Dr Hadzibegovic, who is a military expert. He is not a military expert -- he is the chief justice of his municipality. This is a military matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness, as a judge who lived in the place in 1992, can verify the correctness of the situation. He is just speaking as a witness and I just want to show him the military diagram of Konjic for the same reason that I showed him the previous diagram. It was drawn up by Professor Hadzibegovic and it was tendered into evidence as such, but I would just like this witness, who has personal experience of the situation, to verify its correctness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What pertinence would it have to the military situation? Do you mean that he was part of the system -- military structure, for him to be able to identify this and give evidence about it, when the experts themselves have said things about it. You have had two experts who have made statements about these things. Why do you need a non-expert to come and say anything about it again?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not asking him about the war-time situation, just the diagram of the organisation of power and authority in the municipality and he was part of that power and authority. He had a function to perform within that system. This diagram was drawn up by an expert witness who was an historian. Could he just take a look at the diagram, study it and say whether it is a true representation and that is how it will go down in the transcript. If he cannot give his opinions, if the witness cannot give his opinion, then he will not, so none of these questions refer to military organisation. I merely want to discuss the organisation of power and authority and this document, in Dr Hadzibegovic's dossier, is on pages 312 and 313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may well get the witness to say what he thinks he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask that these diagrams be presented to the witness -- I have a copy for the court, but, as I say, they have already been admitted as diagrams made up by Professor Hadzibegovic. (Handed) Mr. Begtasovic, as a citizen of Konjic and as a man who performed certain duties, do you have personal knowledge as to the organisation of power and authority in Konjic in 1992 -- was it as represented in the diagram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In my answers to the previous questions I gave an affirmative answer to your question and I repeat this affirmative answer. I have in front of me a diagram of the organisation of power and authority in Konjic in the municipality during the war and before the war, when there was the danger of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, Mr. Begtasovic, whether the wartime presidency is a civilian or a military organ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the highest civilian organ in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like to ask you, Mr. Begtasovic, do you personally know Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In performing your duties in Konjic in 1992, did you at any time receive orders from Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, and were you somebody who was subordinate to Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Begtasovic, who were the commanders of the headquarters of Territorial Defence of Konjic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, they were Mr. Ramic, Mr. Boric, and Mr. Catic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your personal knowledge, was Mr. Zejnil Delalic ever commander of the municipal headquarters in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not -- he was never commander of the municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Zejnil Delalic at one time held any military functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that he was commander of a military group. I am not quite sure -- I am not very high up on the structure of military authority, but I seem to recall that he was the commander of a Tactical Group. I am not quite sure of the exact term given to the group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, I am now going to ask you several other questions related to your own personal and professional knowledge. Tell me, please, Mr. Begtasovic, whether members of the Ministry of Internal Affairs can take statements from citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they can take statements. This is colloquially referred to as an "informative dialogue".

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can these statements at any time form the basis for a decision for prosecution -- can they lead to prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These statements can never be a basis for a decision to bring in a case against these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happens to them after they come to court, these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then the judge -- investigating judge -- must, according to the rules, separate these statements and records of the statements in a separate file and they are separately kept as separate files, so that the counsel deliberating and investigating the case does not have these files -- the trial chamber's.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, if the prosecutor ceases to prosecute, what happens to the criminal case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The court in that case severs the criminal proceedings -- puts a stop to the criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Against the same individual, for perpetuating the same crime, can the case be brought up once again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and in this case we are speaking about res judicata. The exception is in the case of a repetition of the criminal proceedings which the court can allow with the adoption of new facts -- if new facts are brought to light -- new evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, which organs issue facts as to whether, before a court, a criminal proceeding is under way or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The courts provide this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to our regulations, do organs exist which have records on the punishment of individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are the organs of internal affairs -- the Ministry of Internal Affairs in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that ministry, at the request of individuals having a legal interest in doing so -- can they issue a confirmation whether an individual has been punished or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but the individual must be able to verify that he has a legal interest in doing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Begtasovic, according to our criminal law, are there crimes for which a Defence counsel is required from the first stages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If there is reasonable doubt that a crime has been committed for which the punishment can be the death penalty, the death sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can the suspect be withheld this right to a Defence attorney?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- to waive this right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does the violation of this right lead to legal repercussions in the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a vital violation of the proceedings and, if it is committed, it will lead to the sentence being revoked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, although you have already said this earlier on, but as I am drawing to the end of my questioning, we have called you here to testify to facts which are directly linked to this case, would you tell us, please, once again whether investigating -- interviewing 105 individuals -- did you question them according to the prevailing rules and regulations and in a legal and lawful manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interviews with the 105 individuals, which I for the most part did, this questioning was done legally, according to all the prevailing rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For reasonable doubt on the basis of the statements of these individuals, were these acts criminal acts according to the laws of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question, although you have partially answered it already, in view of the fact of what you learnt questioning those individuals, was their detention lawful and justified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Begtasovic. I have no further questions, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examination by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, may it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Begtasovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I represent the Defence of Mr. Zdravko Mucic. I do not have many questions for you. However, as a highly qualified witness, as a colleague of ours, as a man of law, I think that you will be able to help us clarify certain facts, which are both relevant and important for determining the truth in these proceedings. I would like to draw your attention, and I am also reminding myself, to the fact that during our exchanges, since we speak the language in which we understand one another, we try to wait until the end of the interpretation of a question into one of the official languages. You wait and then give your answer. Mr. Begtasovic, according to the laws and the rules regulating prisons in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, can we say that, regardless of the fact whether someone had been sentenced by the military or a civilian court, that the sentence was always served in a civilian prison, that is, in a correctional facility which was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice, which was originally called the Secretariat of Justice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, could we further say that by the fall of SFRY the legislation gradually changed and a new one was adopted and that these laws and regulations were not changing rapidly, but, rather, quite gradually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. In the legislation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the proclamation of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent State, first a large number of laws and legal provisions were adopted from the former SFRY and they were adopted as laws and legal provisions of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was in the initial period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can we say that the adoption of these laws and regulations proceeded in such a way that they were purged of Communism of self-management and everything else that dominated the previous system, and this was then adjusted to the circumstances within the republic, that is, the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Begtasovic, during your examination-in-chief, you limited yourself not to tempore criminis suspecti, but until January 1993 when you were involved in the questioning of certain suspects and you said that you did not have knowledge of what went on in 1992, that is, the period between May and November 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, when you conducted questioning, what authorities did you have at that time? Did you have any military rank, a police rank, or was this -- or was it the case that only your expertise was used -- the expertise of somebody who had a long record of experience in criminal affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The latter part of your question is correct -- in fact, I was never in the military, I never served in the military, I never had any rank, so I was simply involved in it as a person who is qualified to question individuals who were suspected of carrying arms and involved in illegal matters and, in that capacity, I was appointed as a member of the Military Investigating Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, if that is so, could you please tell me, when you conducted these interviews, could you, for instance, order the guards who were bringing you these individuals whom you were to question, whether to do certain things or not to do certain things, because I assume these were military personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rule, I could not do this. Obviously, I could request these guards who were guarding these individuals to bring over a person that I was to question, and I could do it and the lady who was the president of the commission could also do it and, in that sense, I had the authority which you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But you could not order these gentlemen to do anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head)

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Could you please state in words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, I could not do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Could you, for instance, order them to tie somebody up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we say, Mr. Begtasovic, that in the Konjic area, and now I am talking about a tempore criminis suspecti, that is, I am talking about this time frame and you were a resident of Konjic, so can we say that in 1992, as the old system broke down, a certain amount of anarchy reigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a certain sense, yes, and I say this taking into account the fact that the court where I worked had no conditions, objectively speaking, to properly work during 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, the suspects whom you questioned later on, that is, in January 1993, were these, for the most part, persons who had been captured during fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you allow for the possibility that some of them may have been captured later, after the fighting stopped, in forests and carrying arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, during your first encounter with these individuals, did you notice that some of them had visible signs or traces of injuries, which they may have sustained either during fighting or during their capture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall seeing such a person, or such persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did individuals whom you questioned complain to you of any such acts against them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What acts?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Acts during their arrest or capture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Begtasovic, let me ask you something else now. Do you know Mr. Zdravko Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just superficially -- I know him by sight, as we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any documents to the effect that Mr. Mucic would have any authority in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Could we say that, during the popular insurrection and crimes committed against the Muslims and roaming of certain groups in the area, people who were in the camp were safer there than being free outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you take as a parameter the number of shells -- it was a higher risk to live in downtown Konjic during the war than in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Begtasovic and, your Honours, thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any further cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I have a few questions, your Honour. May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good morning, judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Back in my country, if you have been a judge for one day, we call you a judge for the rest of your life so I hope you do not mind if I do call you judge, Sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, I am going to ask you some questions in about four areas. I do not think it will take long, but I will just go over those areas with you right now so you know what we are going to be talking about. The first thing I am going to talk to you about is the actual method of questioning these people you questioned as a member of the commission. The second thing I want to talk to you about is the authority in the former Yugoslavia and, also, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for gaolers to take people into custody, and then I want to talk to you about the citizenship laws and nationality laws of the republic, and finally I will ask you about some kinds of records and whether or not you know whether they exist. Sometimes my questions are probably not nearly as artful as yours are. So, if I ask a question you do not understand it, will you stop me and I will repeat it, rephrase it, whatever it takes. The first subject I want to talk to you about, like I said, was the manner in which these statements were taken from those, what, 105, approximately, accused. When you were questioning them, did you see them -- were they tied or shackled or restrained in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The questioning was conducted in the building of the station for public security in Konjic. This is an elevation in town which is called Musala. These individuals were kept in the sports hall which bore the same name, which is Musala. The sports hall -- the distance between the sports hall and the building where the questioning took place was about 100 metres. I recall that, on one occasion, while these individuals were transported from the sports hall to the public security station, these persons were cuffed. As they entered the office where the commission was conducting this questioning, that is, where all the members and the note taker were, these people would be uncuffed for the duration of the questioning. If these personnel who had brought them there, or the personnel of the public security station had not done it previously, they certainly did it once they got there and when I asked them to uncuff them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, let me follow that up just a bit. You have been back in the back here in the Defence room for, what, since I guess last week, and you have seen these four accused being moved by the security guards here, and, when they move them from one place to another outside the courtroom, they are shackled -- you have seen that, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was an identical procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When they were brought into the courtroom, they were unshackled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You did not see any guards or anyone beat people to get statements out of them, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you did not see any big bulky guards standing behind these people, coercing them into giving statements, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, there were no such big bulky persons in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: None of these people who were brought to you looked like they had been beaten up or coerced in any way when they got there, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did you on any occasion interrogate any of these suspects on more than one day, so maybe you talked to them today, send them back to the sports hall and bring them back the next day or a couple of days later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, during a single day, a number of suspects were questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did any of these suspects that you recall complain to you that they had been beaten or threatened to give statements, or that they had been told what to tell you, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would this be a convenient time to take the morning break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good morning again, judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You are correct, I am sorry, it is afternoon. Judge, one last question about the suspects you questioned, and then we will move on to something else. Did any of those people complain to you that they had been somehow mistreated while they were being detained in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, judge. Let us go on to another subject. I want to talk to you a little bit about people who run gaols or prisons. Under the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also under the law of the former Yugoslavia, if a person who was under arrest was delivered to a gaol or a prison -- some kind of confinement facility -- did the head of that gaol or the guards in that gaol, or the deputy head of that gaol have any legal obligation to determine whether or not the person was being legally confined, or could they just simply rely on the fact that the prisoner was brought to them by someone of the appropriate State authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, to determine this fact is under the competencies of the courts. Therefore, the officials of the prison and, even the commander, has no right according to the law to determine whether these individuals, these suspects, have been detained for committing a criminal act or not, whether they have been justly detained or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you a lot, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Was that the answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is exactly the answer I wanted, that gaolers have no legal authority to enquire into the legality of detention. The next thing I want to talk to you about, judge, is the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina as they related to citizenship and nationality -- when I say "nationality", I do not mean ethnic origin. What I mean is the connection between a person and the State, similar to citizenship. Are you familiar with the laws of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as it relates to citizenship and nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If I go outside of your expertise, let me know and we will stop. Back in April 1992, when Bosnia became an independent nation, recognised by the European Community, member of the United Nations, did the republic confer both its citizenship and its nationality on all habitual residents of the republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the individuals who resided within Bosnia-Herzegovina, along with conditions previously determined by law, were citizens of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina up until 1992 -- to be more exact, up to mid April 1992. The question of citizenship was regulated by the law on citizenship for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the law on citizenship of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This latter law was later on taken over by the legal organs of power and authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, at the same time, these two laws, as far as I recall, were in force up until the fall of 1992, when a new law was adopted relating to citizenship for Bosnia-Herzegovina. This law, along with very slight changes, amendments, which came in 1996, as far as I recall, is in force today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If I were a citizen of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 5 April 1992, the day Bosnia became independent, and I lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was a habitual resident of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did I become a citizen of BH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an explicit provision of the law on citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, had you, on 6 April 1992, been a citizen of the SFRJ and if you resided on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And also a national of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, judge, are there provisions in Bosnian law to give up or renounce your Bosnian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber what those provisions were in the period from May through December 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The law provides for several forms -- several procedures for renouncing citizenship, or for it to cease to exist. One is release from citizenship, one is renouncing your -- the second is renouncing your citizenship, and another form is according to an international contract, whereby this can be done. The most complicated form of ceasing to be a citizen is contained in the provision which I mentioned and which refers to renouncement. If necessary, I shall go into an explanation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Unless the Trial Chamber thinks it is necessary, I do not think that is necessary. But the question I do have to follow up is: if a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina wished to give up his citizenship, for whatever reason, and how ever -- in any of the three ways he wanted to do it, would there be some documents on file with the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina showing that he had given up his citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At all events, yes, there would. For somebody to give up his citizenship of any of the three counts, the individual requesting that his citizenship cease in the BH republic must, to the organs of authority, submit a request. The competent authorities will then deliberate on that request and they will either adopt it, or refute it. Therefore, tabling such a request to be released from citizenship does not automatically mean ipso jure, for a given time, that that request is met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If there were these requests made and there were these documents within the republic somewhere, would they be available to, say, the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They could be, because the Prosecutor has the legal interest in obtaining those documents, and the organ in question, by law, is duty bound to give the prosecuting office these documents for insight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, one last area, and then I think we are done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before he goes on, let me ask a question. Are you suggesting that a person who applies to renounce citizenship can be refused? An application for citizenship -- for renouncing citizenship can be refused by the authorities -- is that what you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are absolutely right, your Honour. That is a way in which we can avoid a situation by which apartheid status can be gained -- the intention of all the international conventions is to reduce the number of Stateless persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can carry on, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, judge, Mr. Greaves pointed out one of the last questions I asked may not have been as clear as it could have been. When I asked if the Office of the Prosecutor could obtain copies of these documents renouncing citizenship, by "Office of the Prosecutor" I mean the Office of the Prosecutor for the Tribunal -- those three people sitting over there and their investigators, could they obtain copies of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had in mind those particular prosecutors, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Somebody suggested to me I might have meant the prosecutor in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I just wanted to clear that up. Judge, what kind of records are maintained by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and when I say "the government", I mean in the larger sense, not just the central Government in Sarajevo, but also the municipality, or the districts, to show that someone is a citizen of BH? For instance, you were shown a document a little while ago -- I believe it was Exhibit D160/1, which was a certificate of citizenship. Would there be other documents such as birth certificates showing that someone was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina and, therefore, was a citizen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is a somewhat vague question. You are asking him whether there are records or not and he answered it according to the best of his ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I will move on to another area, your Honour. Judge, in April 1992, when citizenship in the newly independent Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was conferred on the habitual residents, was it conferred without regard to the person's ethnic background or their religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had nothing to do with national or religious affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, when you say "national" there, you mean ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right -- ethnic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you include aliens in this, too, who are habitually living in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- were they also entitled to their citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What "aliens" do you have in mind, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Persons who do not come within any of the boundaries -- they are neither Bosniaks or Serbs, but were merely living there, and not also citizens of SFRY -- anybody else who was habitually living in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the date that the law came into force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regardless of ethnic affiliation, only citizens of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia residing in Bosnia-Herzegovina had the right to citizenship in the new State.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is what I wanted to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McMurrey, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning. I have only a few questions this morning, but on a more promising note, and recognising that today, 6 April, marks the six-year anniversary of the outbreak of the Bosnian war, Konjic municipality is one of the first open cities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, welcoming back Serb families; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And, also, going back to 1992, when the war first broke out in April and May, there was an influx of some 20,000 to 30,000 refugees from eastern Bosnia flowing through Konjic at that time; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is true, and I am a witness of it happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I just want to find out -- but you told us Konjic was blocked from all sides, how could the refugees come in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the forests, across the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour. Did that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: With that influx of refugees at that time, these people came to the city of Konjic telling their stories of murder, rape and destruction of their hometowns, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: And so, in April and May and June of 1992, that brought about a sense of panic and fear in the people of Konjic, that this was maybe about to happen to them; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right there again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to go on to another topic right now. I want to talk about your capacity as an investigating judge in the municipality of Konjic. When you are an investigating judge, this is in the civil law system, not a common law system like we are accustomed to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The system of criminal continental law.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay, that is another name for it, yes, continental law, in which an investigative judge collects information and, under the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina, under your ethical code of conduct for either a lawyer or a judge, it is your duty not to disclose that information collected in your capacity as an investigating judge; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, but may I add something? The law on criminal proceedings, there is a regulation of the law, which expressly forbids any statements to be made as to information received at this particular stage of the investigating process.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to differentiate between your capacity as an investigative judge, where you have a duty not to disclose statements, and your duties under an assignment of a commission, such as the statements that were introduced by Madam Residovic in the Delalic Defence on Friday, which was D149 through to 159, I think -- those were statements taken in your capacity as a member of a commission appointed by a military branch; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: As opposed to statements taken in your capacity as an investigating judge, which are totally not subject to disclosure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examination by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Begtasovic. My name is Giuliano Turone and I am a trial attorney for the Prosecution for this trial. Let me ask you also some questions related to your testimony in chief. You told us that you have been working as a judge in Konjic from 1976 until 1995; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In that period of time, did you also work as an investigating judge for criminal proceedings -- I mean, some time during those years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did also work as an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not get the translation -- could you repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I also worked as an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And when did that happen -- in which years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My basic area is the criminal law, and the procedure that would follow the investigating period. However, I also, during my time as a judge, worked as an investigating judge and I cannot tell you exactly the number of cases that I worked on as an investigating judge and I was involved in that throughout the period that I was a judge in Konjic, that is, 1976 until I stopped being a judge there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I see. So there was not a specific period in which you dealt with the work of an investigating judge only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head) That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Begtasovic, you mentioned that starting in April or May 1992, Konjic was surrounded and then shelled almost daily. Can you say approximately how long did the shelling last in your town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you talking about the daily shellings?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, for how long did these daily shellings go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: For each day, or continuously for how many days?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Let us say for how long a time did continuous relevant shelling daily or almost daily, did that go on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall a single day in 1992, starting in early May, when there was no shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean until the end of the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this distance in time, it seems to me that it went on until the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. You also stated in your examination-in-chief that general mobilisation was proclaimed in Konjic around 20 April 1992, you said, I think. Can you tell us who proclaimed general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency of the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was the war presidency then the competent authority for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because it took over the authority, that is, the competencies of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And to which extent and in which terms did the mobilisation concern you personally -- I mean, what did you do during 1992 after mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had work duty, and it involved the duties which related to my position as the chief judge in Konjic court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You also stated that, because of the shelling, persons could not go to work, and the courts could not function from April 1992 and during the entire year 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But, in any case, would you agree with me that persons did move around Konjic anyway in 1992 and persons did on a more or less regular basis report to duties, including their assignments from the TO and war presidency; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is absolutely true. However, there was one risk involved -- you could have lost your life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I see what you mean, but in any case, even prisoners, would you agree with me, that they were in fact moved to other areas, at least for the purposes of exchange; is that true, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In any case, could you tell us, when did the basic court in Konjic start functioning again and, in particular, when did criminal proceedings start taking place again in the basic court of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, that was at around the same time when the department of the military court started working. Before this took place, the court building was repaired and I would like to point out that they shared the same building, that is, the basic court and the department of the military court of Mostar. During 1992 and in 1993, it was shelled several times, and, as far as I recall, some time in the summer of 1993, this court building was repaired. It was shelled later, too, but at least it was brought to the level when it functioned, so that, in late 1993, we had proceedings going on in the court building, but this is all as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean criminal proceedings in the basic court of Konjic started taking place again after summer of 1993 -- not at the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is correct, and I think it is an insignificant number of cases. I think it was not a very sizeable case load.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. As soon as the basic court started functioning again, what kind of work did you do exactly as far as criminal proceedings were concerned? Did that change something in your personal position in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I should only point out that there were very few new case files which we received; in other words, there were very few lawsuits filed, very few indictments which were referred to the basic court in Konjic. For the most part, these were files that had already been initiated before the war and the bulk of the cases was really relating to the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So, in any case, you mean that your functions were the same after the court functioned again during the entire period of 1992, without any changes in your personal professional position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As soon as the basic court in Konjic started functioning again, how many judges dealt with criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I was the only one. I mentioned earlier in my testimony that, before the war, in addition to me, there was Judge Silic and Judge Smrkic who also dealt with criminal matters but they both left Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened after the summer of 1993 when criminal proceedings started taking place again, could you deal with the criminal matters by yourself, when were there proceedings that had to be dealt with by a panel of judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For those criminal proceedings for which a single judge was appointed, I was dealing with those. However, where there was a Chamber of three -- a panel of three judges involved, then I would have the judges' jury members with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean lay jurors -- not professional judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, lay jurors. The basic courts were established in such a way that a single judge can preside over a proceeding, or a panel of three judges. If there is a panel of three judges, it is always one professional judge and two lay jurors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I see. You also stated that a department or the military court was created in Konjic -- you said around autumn 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness nods head)

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As a judge of the basic court, did you have to perform any duties also within the Konjic department of the military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And who were the judges dealing with that in Konjic -- can you say the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the judges of the military court?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, the Konjic department of the military court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can recall them. I recall a judge whose name was Selejman Bajric. I also remember a judge whose name was Rasim Trnka -- Rasim with an "M" -- R-A-S-I-M -- with an M -- as in "Mostar". Also, a lady judge whose name was Sena Uzunovic and a judge Meho Musinovic, and a judge Reuf Zaimovic. And I remember a judge Jasmin Sose. Those are the judges whose names I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Begtasovic, you stated that, after the combats of May 1992, many persons were arrested for participating in an armed rebellion. Do you know if these persons or any of them would have been entitled to prisoner of war status.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am going to object. That is outside his area of expertise, unless it is shown he has expertise in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I would say that a criminal judge has the knowledge to answer this question, especially a judge who had something to do with these prisoners in the commission of the fourth court. May I invite the witness to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The judge may not be well versed with international law. When you talk about prisoners of war you are talking in terms of Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How would he know that? What would his expertise be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I would say the commission of the 4th Corps, who had to investigate the prisoners as we heard in the testimony in chief, implied work which had something to do with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask him perhaps whether he knows the circumstances in which they were brought to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know the circumstances in which these persons were brought to proceedings? If you do not know about the applicability of the prisoners of war status, you can say that, anyway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the court's permission, I would prefer not to offer my opinion on that question, precisely for reasons which you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: all right. May I ask that Defence Exhibit D7/1 be shown again to the witness, please? (Handed) You stated that this document, which is dated 5 January 1993, is the order by which you were appointed as a member of the 4th Corps Commission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who signed this order, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who signed it. Here it states that the person who issued the order is a Major Mirsad Catic. However, before his name, there is a preposition "for", which means that someone else signed this document -- not he himself and I do not know who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Anyway, in which capacity did Mr. Catic or somebody else for him sign that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In any event, in the capacity of the commander of the municipal staff of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. So, according to point 4 of this order, Mr. Begtasovic, you had to give a report after completing your work. Did you see point 4? My question is: did you give such a final report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see point 4 and I do understand what your question is. Concerning the work duties contained in point 4, to be honest with you, I do not recall my own participation in compiling the report that is mentioned here. Usually, the report is drafted by one person. I assume that Ms. Jasminka Dzumhur, the president of the commission, did that. I assume the report was drafted and that the other members of the commission signed it. However, at this point, I do not recall the contents of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean that this report was given and that you did not sign it, or this report was given and you signed it as well and do not remember -- could you please clarify that a little?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been normal for me to have signed it as well as all the other members of the commission and I believe that that is what actually happened. I doubt that the report was signed only by the president of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that you are saying that the report was given -- you signed it, and you do not remember the contents of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you with absolute certainty even whether I had signed it. I assumed that this was done and I do not remember the contents of this report at this time. If you showed me this report with my signature on it, I probably would recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The problem is that we did not see any report like that, neither coming from the Defence or her Defence military witness. This is why I wanted to ask you something about this report nobody is talking about. In any case, let us clarify something. The report was given, and, even if you do not remember whether you signed it or not, and even if you do not remember the contents of it, could you say approximately when was it given?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did he say the report was given?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He does not even remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: He said the report was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: "Must have been given", he says -- "it must have been given", and he thinks he must have signed it also, but he does not remember now. That is his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Let me say then, you have no possibility to say anything else but that -- that you do not remember whether there was a report, whether you signed it, and, if there was a report, you do not remember the contents -- is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fair statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In any case, Mr. Begtasovic, in consideration of point 4 of this appointment order, you members of the commission were supposed to find out how many prisoners were subject to court proceedings and if you read again point 4, how many proceedings were subject to court proceedings, how many were not subject to court proceedings, how many were wounded and sick, and how many had incurable wounds and diseases; is that correct?
