utterances.text: I have heard your decision, but I ask the question so that we should know, because in the transcript it said that on Monday our colleagues would continue the cross-examination -- the Brigadier was present and I would just like to say that the Brigadier has a visa lasting 50 days. The visa expires on the 9th, so as he is the first witness here, the prime witness, this makes a difficulty with his stay in Holland. But we must respect the court's decision, although it has been 11 days since the colleagues and the Prosecutor has all the material at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There are good reasons why he should be in Holland and The Hague. I think the visa will be accordingly extended to cover the period. Let us have your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like the next witness for the Defence to be called. He is Arif Sultanic. Before the witness enters, could I just ask you whether we are going to complete this witness and then continue the Brigadier's cross-examination, so I can tell the witness, or are we going to interrupt the examination of this witness? I would like to have the examination done as a whole, without any interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You could interrupt his examination-in-chief to enable the cross-examine to be completed. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We would continue - we do not want to lost any time. Whatever time we have, we will use it up and carry on. On Thursday, we will start with the cross-examination. It is only the Prosecutor and then the other Defence counsel who have also reserved their cross-examination. It will not be as tedious as you are expecting. With the thorough study as I see the Prosecutor is doing, he might know how to organise himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, now I am clear on procedure, because I have an obligation towards my witnesses to tell them the order in which they are going to be examined and re-examined. May I call the witness now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, kindly invite the witness in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can take your seat, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Sir. Would you tell the Chamber your name and surname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Arif Sultanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, before I start my questioning, I should like to warn you of a technical aspect of this hearing. You and I both speak the same language and we could ask questions and give answers very quickly, but, in the booths that you see up there, we have our interpreters, who are doing a very difficult job, to translate for the Chamber everything that we are talking about here. That is why I should like to ask you, Mr. Sultanic, to pay attention to the earphones you have on the table beside you and, when I ask a question, you are going to hear the translation of my question. After you hear the interpreters have finished, then you can take up my question and answer it so that everybody in the Chamber will be able to hear and understand us. Have I been clear enough, Mr. Sultanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, tell me when you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 25 February 1946.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the court where you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in a village near the town of Konjic in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you live, Mr. Sultanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I live in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What citizenship do you hold, Mr. Sultanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have Bosnian and Herzegovinian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am, by profession, an electrical engineer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What education do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to primary school in Konjic, secondary school in Sarajevo, and I went to university in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you work -- where did your work take you, professionally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a time, I worked in Mostar, then I worked in Sarajevo, and, until the conflicts broke out, I worked in Konjic. My main office was in Mostar, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What work were you engaged in, Mr. Sultanic, immediately before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, immediately prior to 6 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked as the head of the working unit and the speciality was the maintenance of the signal and security installations and tele command for communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at the same time, Mr. Sultanic, have your own private business, to call it that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, prior to the conflict, I got the material necessary and equipment I needed for household appliance maintenance, that is to say, television sets, video recorders, and other similar appliances.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was your sojourn on 6 April 1992 -- where exactly were you residing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Near the railway station; the street was Proleterskih Brigada, number 8 -- Proletarian Brigade, number 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, as a citizen of Konjic, can you tell the court what ethnic groups did the population of Konjic belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The population of Konjic was composed of all types of nations -- there were Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Jews, and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have the exact figures before us on the record about the population percentages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, Mr. Sultanic, in view of the fact that you worked for the railways, did you at any time -- did, in April 1992 -- was road traffic interrupted in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Road traffic was interrupted towards Sarajevo in the section between Ivan Planina and Bradina and on the road towards Mostar at the end of April it was severed at Aleksin Han -- it is a bridge of the Grabavica Lake and lower down, some 20 kilometres away, the Bijela bridge, which bridges a bay from the Lakovacko Lake.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Sultanic, I said as you worked for the railways, because road traffic was severed. Let me now ask you, as you did work for the railways, where the -- was railway traffic interrupted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 27 April of that year, 1992, railway lines towards Sarajevo from the direction of Konjic were severed. Later on, at the beginning of May, railway links were interrupted towards Mostar -- with the destruction of the railway bridge at the outskirts of Mostar. The bridge crossed the Neretva River.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sultanic, as this is your particular speciality, can you tell us what links the town of Konjic had in the course of April with other parts of the republic, and with the capital -- in April, that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April, the town had telephone communications with Sarajevo -- the PTT links, communications. Railway lines were severed when there was no railway traffic. The railway system had its own system of telephone communications parallel with the system of the Post Telephone and Telegraph communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the PTT communications of the town of Konjic were severed with the capital, when were the PTT communications between Sarajevo and Konjic severed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that -- on 2 May 1992, the day that the President of the republic was taken prisoner, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and the main post office in Sarajevo was set fire to, so that, with that act, all links and communications between Sarajevo and the world and, of course, between Sarajevo and other towns in the republic, were severed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, at one time in May 1992, was the town of Konjic -- did the town of Konjic lose its post and telecommunication links with other parts of the republic and not only with the capital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said so a moment ago. I said that all links towards Mostar were severed with the destruction of the railway bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why, for the interruption of telecommunications, would the destruction of a railway bridge near the town of Mostar be relevant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the cables linking the PTT centres went via the railway bridge, together with our railway cables -- the same route was followed, because otherwise, from Sarajevo to Mostar, the same channel contained the PTT and the railway cables in order to save on construction work -- this was one communications line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, at the beginning of 1992, in addition to this blockade, the one you have just explained to us, was your town shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes, there was shelling of Konjic on 4 May of that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How frequently and for what duration was Konjic shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Konjic was shelled from that day, every day, at least twice a day and, very often, during the night as well, so that I do not remember a single day when the town was not shelled from the day you mentioned until the agreement was signed -- until the Dayton agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sultanic, tell us, please, whether, some time during May and April 1992, the roads towards the surrounding villages were blocked as well -- villages around Konjic, in the surrounds of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. In that month, roads were blocked along Donje Selo, which links the south-westerly villages with the town of Konjic. They are Kralupi, Hasinovice, Balmis, Dabovice, Irici, Tresnejavica, and towards the west Lisicici, and west of Lisicici, Nevizdraci, Obre towards Butrovic Polje and the River Neretva -- those are the villages -- towards Sarajevo the Bradina road was blocked, whereas towards the southern portions of the Konjic municipality, the road to Bijela, to Ravni Kuk was blocked in the direction of Borci, on the one hand and, on the other side of Borci, the road was blocked near the village of Glavaticevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, whether at the same time these blockades took place, if you know of this, whether at the same time that these blockades took place, that the population was expelled from the surrounding villages -- if you know anything about this, please tell us what the population was and who did the expelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the population was expelled -- the Bosnians were expelled from the village of Bijela -- that is one village and two other villages are Dzajici and Gakici and upstream towards the river Neretva, towards Borci.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In May, and in the rest of 1992, what were the supplies like for the town -- do you know what the supply situation was like for the town and its population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, although this was not my -- within my realm of activity, but I do know that the population had to wait in long lines in front of the Caritas and Red Cross organisation and the Merhamet and the food that did manage to reach the town via Croatia and Herzegovina to Konjic were distributed in front of the Caritas, Merhamet and the Red Cross organisations and part of the population had some stores at home. They had stockpiled, so they were able to take in some of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have completed my general questions. I would now like to move to my other questions. Perhaps it is time to complete the examination for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until the 9th, Thursday, possibly after the cross-examination. So we will adjourn until 10am on Thursday. (At 5.30pm the hearing adjourned until Thursday, 9 April 1997, at 10am) 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon luncheon adjournment taken at 1 p.m
